endorsements.quote: (5) Inference-from-Outputs Testing: Researchers can analyze model outputs or embeddings to determine what protected attributes or unintended information can be back-inferred or “leaked” through outputs, pointing to targets for refining privacy and consent protections.

(2) Adversarial and Stress Testing: Researchers can use adversarial inputs, i.e., deliberately constructed perturbations or inputs designed to expose model vulnerabilities, problematic decision boundaries, or sensitive inference pathways [ 41 , 42 ].

Clinicians or designated clinical reviewers should verify AI-generated or AI-assisted outputs before they are incorporated into the patient record or relied upon for care, with the verification status and reviewer identity preserved as part of the object’s metadata.
Model developers should document performance characteristics, intended-use limits, training and validation conditions, and known failure modes.
For AI-generated or AI-assisted clinical text, metadata should preserve source inputs, model version, human reviewer, substantive edits, verification status, and final sign-off.

The shifting nature of these capacities calls for dynamic and granular consent processes [ 47 , 48 ] that enable individuals – or communities of individuals – to revisit consent and de-select certain forms of data sharing if they are empirically demonstrated to carry higher risks of re-identification or downstream harms.

Tracking the trajectories of latent embeddings, derived risk scores, synthetic images, or other model-generated attributes creates shared accountability by documenting where they originate, how they are transformed, and where they are ultimately used.
We propose that provenance labeling for MMAI-generated data be treated as a foundational requirement rather than an optional transparency measure.

unlisted_practices: Store model-generated data in the EHR with structured metadata identifying its synthetic origin, the producing model, source inputs, and generation date.
EHR certification standards should require provenance metadata to be preserved across data transfers, exports, and downstream reuse.
Institutions using MMAI-generated data in model training should document and disclose the proportion of synthetic inputs in training sets.
Give clinicians the ability to annotate or correct model-generated interpretations before record entry.
Give patients a meaningful pathway to dispute generated inferences or documentation that misrepresents them.
Researchers should build and publicly disseminate a continuously updated evidence base or registry of multimodal inference capacities and risks.
The FDA should incorporate multimodal inference testing into premarket review for higher-risk clinical applications.
Standards bodies such as NIST should develop shared benchmarks and evaluation resources for independent assessment of multimodal inference.
Generate multimodal inferences or synthesize data only when scientifically or clinically justified, with input from ethicists, technologists, legal experts, and affected communities.

Use privacy-preserving techniques such as differential privacy, feature-level transformations, obfuscation, and machine unlearning to limit unjustified inferences, balancing privacy against utility using evidence-based thresholds.
Assess the verification labor and hidden burdens of AI efficiency gains before adopting MMAI documentation or diagnostic tools.
Use federated learning or distributed training to reduce traceability of multimodal inferences to individuals.

screen.reason: This is a perspective/commentary proposing an ethical and governance agenda (provenance labeling, dynamic consent, privacy-preserving techniques) for multimodal AI in healthcare.
